Appendix J Reward Hacking Analysis Proofs

Here we provide a theoretical analysis motivating PBRR, relying on different assumptions than the regret analysis in Section 4. We show that PBRR’s repaired reward function is guaranteed to induce an optimal policy that matches or exceeds the performance of the reference policy (Thm. 4.3) and resolve two specific instantiations of reward hacking (Cors. 4.4, 4.5) in the infinite data setting as the number of iterations goes to infinity.

J.1 Assumptions

For this theoretical analysis we assume all of the assumptions listed in Section J. Below we expand on the assumption that preferences are labeled by regret.

We define regret under r~\tilde{r} for a trajectory τ=(s0,a0,…,sH)\tau=(s_{0},a_{0},\ldots,s_{H}) as regret⁡(τ∣r~)≜∑t=0|τ|−1γt​[Vr~∗​(st)−Qr~∗​(st,at)]=∑t=0|τ|−1(−γt​Ar~∗​(st,at))\mathrm{regret}(\tau\mid\tilde{r})\;\triangleq\;\sum_{t=0}^{|\tau|-1}\gamma^{t}\!\left[V^{*}_{\tilde{r}}(s_{t})-Q^{*}_{\tilde{r}}(s_{t},a_{t})\right]\;=\;\sum_{t=0}^{|\tau|-1}\!\left(-\gamma^{t}A^{*}_{\tilde{r}}(s_{t},a_{t})\right) where Ar~∗​(s,a)≜Qr~∗​(s,a)−Vr~∗​(s)A^{*}_{\tilde{r}}(s,a)\!\triangleq\!Q^{*}_{\tilde{r}}(s,a)-V^{*}_{\tilde{r}}(s) and Vr~∗,Qr~∗V^{*}_{\tilde{r}},Q^{*}_{\tilde{r}} are the optimal value and action-value functions under r~\tilde{r}. We then assume a preference between τ1\tau_{1} and τ2\tau_{2} is determined by regret:

μ≜{0if ​regret​(τ1|r)<regret⁡(τ2|r),1if ​regret​(τ1|r)>regret⁡(τ2|r),12if ​regret​(τ1|r)=regret⁡(τ2|r),\mu\triangleq\begin{cases}0&\text{if }\mathrm{regret}(\tau_{1}|r)<\mathrm{regret}(\tau_{2}|r),\\ 1&\text{if }\mathrm{regret}(\tau_{1}|r)>\mathrm{regret}(\tau_{2}|r),\\ \frac{1}{2}&\text{if }\mathrm{regret}(\tau_{1}|r)=\mathrm{regret}(\tau_{2}|r),\end{cases} (42)

where regret is the sum of negative optimal advantage:

regret(τ∣r~)≜∑t=0|τ|−1−Ar~∗(stτ,atτ).\displaystyle\mathrm{regret}(\tau\mid\tilde{r})\triangleq\sum_{t=0}^{|\tau|-1}-A^{*}_{\tilde{r}}(s_{t}^{\tau},a_{t}^{\tau}).

We also assume ℒpref\mathcal{L}_{\text{pref}} uses regret-based preferences.

Knox et al. (2022) shows that human preferences are better described by the difference in regret between trajectory segments, as opposed to the difference in the sum of rewards. In practice, we simulate human preference labels using the difference in sum of rewards between trajectories because regret is intractable to compute in our empirical environments, as discussed in Appendix A.

Our assumption about how preferences are labeled (Eq. 42) for this analysis differs in two key ways from Knox et al. (2022): (i) we assume preferences are over trajectories, not trajectory segments (ii) we assume preferences are noiselessly determined by regret, not sampled from a Boltzmann distribution. Our analysis holds without assumption (i) as long as preferences are elicited over an exhaustive set of trajectory segments. We argue that (ii) is a reasonable assumption when executing PBRR, where preferences are only collected between trajectories sampled from πr^t\pi_{\hat{r}_{t}}—which is initially substantially sub-optimal due to a misspecified proxy reward function r^t\hat{r}_{t}, and πref\pi_{\text{ref}}—which is assumed to be a safe policy. There is clear distinction between the trajectories from these policies—both qualitatively and in terms of regret under rr, so we assume no preference noise via Eq. 42.

We also assume that all trajectories begin from the same start state s0s_{0}. This assumption is without loss of generality: for any MDP with initial state distribution p0p_{0}, we can construct an equivalent MDP by introducing a new start state s0′s^{\prime}_{0} that transitions in a single step according to p0p_{0}. In this construction, all trajectories then originate from s0′s^{\prime}_{0}, satisfying the assumption of a single start state.

J.2 Proof of Theorem 4.3

Lemma J.1.

Suppose Assumptions 4.5 and 4.6 hold. Then the repaired reward function r^\hat{r} and the ground-truth reward function rr induce identical regret-based orderings on all inter-policy trajectory pairs (τ1,τ2)∈𝒯πr^∗×𝒯πref(\tau_{1},\tau_{2})\in\mathcal{T}_{\pi^{*}_{\hat{r}}}\times\mathcal{T}_{\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}}:

sign⁡[regret⁡(τ1∣r^)−regret⁡(τ2∣r^)]=sign⁡[regret⁡(τ1∣r)−regret⁡(τ2∣r)].\mathrm{sign}\left[\mathrm{regret}(\tau_{1}\mid\hat{r})-\mathrm{regret}(\tau_{2}\mid\hat{r})\right]=\mathrm{sign}\left[\mathrm{regret}(\tau_{1}\mid r)-\mathrm{regret}(\tau_{2}\mid r)\right].
Proof.

Let (τ1,τ2)∈(τ1,τ2)∈𝒯πr^∗×𝒯πref(\tau_{1},\tau_{2})\in(\tau_{1},\tau_{2})\in\mathcal{T}_{\pi^{*}_{\hat{r}}}\times\mathcal{T}_{\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}} denote an arbitrary inter-policy trajectory pair. Define the Bayes optimal decision rule for distinguishing preferences as

f0/1∗​(τ1,τ2,r)≜{1if ​p​(1∣τ1,τ2,r)>p⁡(−1∣τ1,τ2,r),0if ​p​(1∣τ1,τ2,r)=p⁡(−1∣τ1,τ2,r),−1if ​p​(1∣τ1,τ2,r)<p⁡(−1∣τ1,τ2,r),f^{*}_{0/1}(\tau_{1},\tau_{2};r)\triangleq\begin{cases}1&\text{if }p(1\mid\tau_{1},\tau_{2},r)>p(-1\mid\tau_{1},\tau_{2},r),\\ 0&\text{if }p(1\mid\tau_{1},\tau_{2},r)=p(-1\mid\tau_{1},\tau_{2},r),\\ -1&\text{if }p(1\mid\tau_{1},\tau_{2},r)<p(-1\mid\tau_{1},\tau_{2},r),\end{cases}

where p⁡(1∣τ1,τ2,r)p(1\mid\tau_{1},\tau_{2},r) denotes the probability that τ1\tau_{1} is preferred to τ2\tau_{2} under the ground-truth reward rr. Under Assumption 4.6, preferences are noiselessly determined by regret, i.e.

p⁡(1∣τ1,τ2,r)={1if ​regret​(τ1∣r)<regret⁡(τ2∣r),12if ​regret​(τ1∣r)=regret⁡(τ2∣r),0if ​regret​(τ1∣r)>regret⁡(τ2∣r).p(1\mid\tau_{1},\tau_{2},r)=\begin{cases}1&\text{if }\mathrm{regret}(\tau_{1}\mid r)<\mathrm{regret}(\tau_{2}\mid r),\\ \frac{1}{2}&\text{if }\mathrm{regret}(\tau_{1}\mid r)=\mathrm{regret}(\tau_{2}\mid r),\\ 0&\text{if }\mathrm{regret}(\tau_{1}\mid r)>\mathrm{regret}(\tau_{2}\mid r).\end{cases}

Now, under Assumption 4.5, the PBRR loss (Eq. 3) reduces in the limit to the standard preference cross-entropy loss (Eq. 1):

limt→∞ℒ⁡(g,r^proxy,𝒟)=ℒpref​(r^proxy+g,𝒟).\lim_{t\to\infty}\mathcal{L}(g;\hat{r}_{\text{proxy}},\mathcal{D})=\mathcal{L}_{\text{pref}}(\hat{r}_{\text{proxy}}+g;\mathcal{D}).

Since cross-entropy is a convex margin loss known to be Bayes consistent (Zhang, 2004; Bartlett et al., 2006), any minimizer r^\hat{r} of ℒpref\mathcal{L}_{\text{pref}} must induce a predictor fℒpref∗f^{*}_{\mathcal{L}_{\text{pref}}} whose sign agrees with the Bayes optimal rule:

sign⁡[fℒpref∗​(τ1,τ2)]=f0/1∗​(τ1,τ2,r).\mathrm{sign}\left[f^{*}_{\mathcal{L}_{\text{pref}}}(\tau_{1},\tau_{2})\right]=f^{*}_{0/1}(\tau_{1},\tau_{2};r).

Substituting the regret-based form of f0/1∗f^{*}_{0/1}, it follows that the ordering induced by r^\hat{r} must coincide with that induced by rr. Equivalently,

sign⁡[regret⁡(τ1∣r^)−regret⁡(τ2∣r^)]=sign⁡[regret⁡(τ1∣r)−regret⁡(τ2∣r)].\mathrm{sign}\left[\mathrm{regret}(\tau_{1}\mid\hat{r})-\mathrm{regret}(\tau_{2}\mid\hat{r})\right]=\mathrm{sign}\left[\mathrm{regret}(\tau_{1}\mid r)-\mathrm{regret}(\tau_{2}\mid r)\right].

∎

Restatement of Theorem 4.3.

Suppose Assumptions 4.5 through 4.9 hold, then the optimal policy for the repaired reward function πr^∗\pi^{*}_{\hat{r}} matches or outperforms the reference policy in the limit as t→∞t\to\infty:

Jr​(πr^∗)≥Jr​(πref).\displaystyle J_{r}(\pi^{*}_{\hat{r}})\geq J_{r}(\pi_{\text{ref}}).
Proof.

Pick any τ1∈𝒯πr^∗\tau_{1}\in\mathcal{T}_{\pi^{*}_{\hat{r}}} and τ2∈𝒯ref\tau_{2}\in\mathcal{T}_{\text{ref}}. By the optimality of πr^∗\pi^{*}_{\hat{r}} under r^\hat{r}:

regret⁡(τ1∣r^)=0≤regret⁡(τ2∣r^).\mathrm{regret}(\tau_{1}\mid\hat{r})=0\;\leq\;\mathrm{regret}(\tau_{2}\mid\hat{r}).

By Lemma J.1, this inequality is preserved under rr, so

regret⁡(τ1∣r)≤regret⁡(τ2∣r).\mathrm{regret}(\tau_{1}\mid r)\;\leq\;\mathrm{regret}(\tau_{2}\mid r).

Note that this implies

maxτ1⁡regret⁡(τ1∣r)≤minτ2⁡regret⁡(τ2∣r).\max_{\tau_{1}}\mathrm{regret}(\tau_{1}\mid r)\;\leq\;\min_{\tau_{2}}\mathrm{regret}(\tau_{2}\mid r).

On the left hand side, the maximum is an upper bound to the expectation over τ1∈𝒯πr^∗\tau_{1}\in\mathcal{T}_{\pi^{*}_{\hat{r}}}, and the minimum is a lower bound to the expectation over τ2∈𝒯πref\tau_{2}\in\mathcal{T}_{\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}}:

𝔼τ1∈𝒯πr^∗​[regret⁡(τ1∣r)]≤maxτ1⁡regret⁡(τ1∣r)≤minτ2⁡regret⁡(τ2∣r)≤𝔼τ2∈𝒯πref​[regret⁡(τ2∣r)].\mathbb{E}_{\tau_{1}\in\mathcal{T}_{\pi^{*}_{\hat{r}}}}\!\big[\mathrm{regret}(\tau_{1}\mid r)\big]\leq\max_{\tau_{1}}\mathrm{regret}(\tau_{1}\mid r)\;\leq\;\min_{\tau_{2}}\mathrm{regret}(\tau_{2}\mid r)\leq\mathbb{E}_{\tau_{2}\in\mathcal{T}_{\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}}}\!\big[\mathrm{regret}(\tau_{2}\mid r)\big].

Therefore, by Assumption 4.8,

𝔼τ1∼πr^∗​[regret⁡(τ1∣r)]≤𝔼τ2∼πref​[regret⁡(τ2∣r)].\mathbb{E}_{\tau_{1}\sim{\pi^{*}_{\hat{r}}}}\!\big[\mathrm{regret}(\tau_{1}\mid r)\big]\;\leq\;\mathbb{E}_{\tau_{2}\sim{\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}}}\!\big[\mathrm{regret}(\tau_{2}\mid r)\big].

Under the single-start-state assumption (Assumption 4.9),

𝔼τ∼π​[regret⁡(τ∣r)]=Vr∗​(s0)−Vrπ​(s0).\mathbb{E}_{\tau\sim\pi}\!\big[\mathrm{regret}(\tau\mid r)\big]\;=\;V_{r}^{*}(s_{0})-V_{r}^{\pi}(s_{0}).

Substituting this identity and rearranging gives

Vr∗​(s0)−Vrπr^∗​(s0)≤Vr∗​(s0)−Vrπref​(s0).V_{r}^{*}(s_{0})-V_{r}^{\pi^{*}_{\hat{r}}}(s_{0})\;\leq\;V_{r}^{*}(s_{0})-V_{r}^{\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}}(s_{0}).

Rearranging terms again gives

Vrπr^∗​(s0)≥Vrπref​(s0)V_{r}^{\pi^{*}_{\hat{r}}}(s_{0})\;\geq\;V_{r}^{\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}}(s_{0})

which is equivalent to

Jr​(πr^∗)≥Jr​(πref).J_{r}(\pi^{*}_{\hat{r}})\;\geq\;J_{r}(\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}).

∎

J.3 Theorem 4.3, Corollary 4.4

Skalse et al. (2022) defines reward hacking as:

Definition J.2.

(Skalse et al., 2022) A pair of reward functions (r~1,r~2)(\tilde{r}_{1},\tilde{r}_{2}) is hackable relative to a policy set Π\Pi and an environment (S,A,T,γ,p0,_)(S,A,T,\gamma,p_{0},\textunderscore) if there exists π,π′∈Π\pi,\pi^{\prime}\in\Pi such that

Jr~1​(π)>Jr~1​(π′)​ and ​Jr~2​(π)<Jr~2​(π′)\displaystyle J_{\tilde{r}_{1}}(\pi)>J_{\tilde{r}_{1}}(\pi^{\prime})\text{ and }J_{\tilde{r}_{2}}(\pi)<J_{\tilde{r}_{2}}(\pi^{\prime})

This canonical definition of reward hacking intuitively states that, if (r~1,r~2)(\tilde{r}_{1},\tilde{r}_{2}) is not hackable given a set of policies Π\Pi , then there does not exist any pair of policies in Π\Pi such that one policy has a strictly higher expected return under r~1\tilde{r}_{1} while the other has a strictly higher expected return under r~2\tilde{r}_{2}. Framed differently, any increase in expected return under r~1\tilde{r}_{1} from switching policies in Π\Pi never decreases the expected return under r~2\tilde{r}_{2}. This definition is particularly strict, as noted by Skalse et al. (2022).

The proof for Corollary 4.4 immediately follows from Theorem 4.3 that if 𝒦⁡(r^,r,𝒯πr^∗∪𝒯πref)=1\mathcal{K}(\hat{r},r;\,\mathcal{T}_{\pi^{*}_{\hat{r}}}\cup\mathcal{T}_{\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}})=1 and we define the set of policies as

Π={πref}∪Πr^∗,\Pi\;=\;\{\pi_{\text{ref}}\}\,\cup\,\Pi^{*}_{\hat{r}},

where Πr^∗\Pi^{*}_{\hat{r}} denotes the set of all policies optimal for r^\hat{r}, then the pair (r^,r)(\hat{r},r) is not hackable relative to Π\Pi under Definition J.2.

J.4 Theorem 4.3, Corollary 4.5

Laidlaw et al. (2024) define reward hacking as:

Definition J.3.

(Laidlaw et al., 2024) Suppose r~\tilde{r} is a ρ\rho-correlated proxy66 6 For the full definition of ρ\rho-correlation, we refer readers to the original paper from Laidlaw et al. (2024). with respect to πref\pi_{\text{ref}}. The proxy reward function is hackable with respect to the ground-truth reward function and πref\pi_{\text{ref}} if,

Jr​(πr~∗)<Jr​(πref).\displaystyle J_{r}(\pi^{*}_{\tilde{r}})<J_{r}(\pi_{\text{ref}}).

This definition of reward hacking only considers reward functions that are reasonable optimization targets, i.e., by requiring the inputted reward function to be ρ\rho-correlated with the ground-truth reward function, and sets a threshold for reward hacking via the expected return of the reference policy under the ground-truth reward function. This definition is less strict than that of Skalse et al. (2022); see Laidlaw et al. (2024) for an in-depth comparison,

The proof for Corollary 4.5 immediately follows from Theorem 4.3 that if 𝒦⁡(r^,r,𝒯πr^∗∪𝒯πref)=1\mathcal{K}(\hat{r},r;\,\mathcal{T}_{\pi^{*}_{\hat{r}}}\cup\mathcal{T}_{\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}})=1, then r^\hat{r} is not hackable with respect to rr and πref\pi_{\text{ref}} under Definition J.3.

Appendix K Plotting Details and Aditional Results

K.1 Plotting details

For Figures 2 and 3, for each seed we roll out a policy for the number of episodes specified in Appendix Table 5. We compute the mean return over all episodes with respect to the ground-truth reward function. We then scale the mean return for policy π\pi as follows:

J^r-scaled​(π)=J^​(π)−J^r​(πref)J^r​(πr∗)−J^r​(πref):\hat{J}_{\text{$r$-scaled}}(\pi)=\frac{\hat{J}(\pi)-\hat{J}_{r}(\pi_{\text{ref}})}{\hat{J}_{r}(\pi^{*}_{r})-\hat{J}_{r}(\pi_{\text{ref}})}:

where J^r\hat{J}_{r} is the empirical mean return under the ground-truth reward function rr. We clip J^r-scaled​(π)\hat{J}_{\text{$r$-scaled}}(\pi) to be in range [−1,1][-1,1]. We perform this clipping for visual clarity, noting that any policy with a scaled return less than 00 does worse than the supplied reference policy, and any policy with a scaled return less than −1-1 is considerably sub-optimal. In Figures 2 and 3, we plot the resulting mean scaled return over 3 seeds.

K.2 Retraining a policy with an updated proxy reward function

McKinney et al. (2023) show that reward functions learned online from human feedback can fail to re-train new policies initialized from scratch with a different random seed. To test whether PBRR’s updated proxy reward function exhibits similar fragility, we reinitialize new policies with different seeds and train the policies using the repaired reward functions learned in Section 5. We also extend PPO training beyond the number of PPO steps used when learning the additive correction term with PBRR, probing whether the updated proxy reward function could induce undesirable behavior if optimized for longer. Figure 8 presents these results: in the Traffic Control, Glucose Monitoring, and Pandemic environments, retraining with the repaired proxy reward function still yield policies that induce near-optimal performance. In the Pandemic Mitigation environment, training PPO for more steps even yields an improvement. In the Glucose Monitoring environment, however, the performance of the policy induced by the repaired proxy reward function deteriorates when trained with substantially more RL steps than were used during reward learning. These findings broadly suggest that PBRR’s repaired proxy reward function is robust to policy reinitialization and to longer RL optimization, but the number of RL steps used while updating the proxy reward function can play a critical role in determining whether the learned signal remains valid under extended training. In other words, when re-training a new policy with a repaired proxy reward function, it is likely best to train that policy with the same number of RL steps as used when repairing the proxy reward function.

K.3 Comparisons against baselines that update πref\pi_{\text{ref}}

Figure 2 compares PBRR against the Online-State-Constraint and RRM + State-Constraint baselines respectively, which each constrain the learned policy to πref\pi_{\text{ref}}. Section D details these baseline implementations. Here we compare PBRR against those baselines, except we update πref\pi_{\text{ref}} every iteration to be the policy constructed at the previous iteration as outlined in Section D. We refer to these additional baselines as Online-RLHF + Moving-State-Constraint and RRM + Moving-State-Constraint.

Our goal with these additional baselines is to attempt to overcome a fundamental limitation of the Online-State-Constraint and RRM + State-Constraint baselines, namely that they may fundamentally limit the performance of the induced policy by penalizing divergences from a fixed πref\pi_{\text{ref}}. Figure 9 below shows that updating πref\pi_{\text{ref}} as described in Section D does not lead to a substantial improvement in performance; PBRR still remains the most performant approach in all environments.

K.4 Ablating PBRR’s regularization terms

PBRR’s preference learning objective in Eq. 3 consists of two regularization terms, ℒ−\mathcal{L}^{-} and ℒ+\mathcal{L}^{+}. In Figure 3 we empirically show that, without these regularization terms, PBRR performs relatively poorly in both stability and achieved mean return. Here we investigate the individual impact of ℒ−\mathcal{L}^{-} and ℒ+\mathcal{L}^{+} respectively. Figure 10 illustrates that PBRR with both regularization terms matches or outperforms all alternatives across environments. The relative effect of using only ℒ−\mathcal{L}^{-} or ℒ+\mathcal{L}^{+} is environment dependent. PBRR’s performance is only degraded by removing a regularization term in the Pandemic Control and Glucose Monitoring environment: removing ℒ+\mathcal{L}^{+} causes the larger drop in Pandemic, while removing ℒ−\mathcal{L}^{-} has the greater effect in Glucose.

K.5 PBRR with intra-policy preferences

PBRR, as implemented for the results in Section 5, elicits preferences over trajectory pairs where one trajectory is sampled from πr^t\pi_{\hat{r}_{t}} and the other from πref\pi_{\text{ref}}. Here we investigate adding intra-policy preferences, i.e., preferences over trajectory pairs where both trajectories are sampled from πr^t\pi_{\hat{r}_{t}}. Figure 11 plots the results when half of the elicited batch is intra-policy preferences. We find that including these preferences degrades data-efficiency and stability. In particular, the performance in the early iterations of the PBRR + intra-policy preferences approach is worse than PBRR in the AI Safety Gridworld and Pandemic environment, and performance decreases in later iterations in the Glucose environment. For the Pandemic environment, PBRR + intra-policy preferences eventually outperforms PBRR, suggesting a potential benefit to including intra-policy preferences. Future work should explore how to leverage this additional data to improve PBRR’s performance without reducing data-efficiency or learning stability in environments where PBRR already performs well.

K.6 Unscaled Main Results

In Figures 2 and 3 we scale and clip the plotted mean return, as detailed in Appendix K.1, for clearer visual comparison. In Figure 12(a) we plot the unclipped, unscaled mean-return for PBRR and the baselines that learn a reward function ab initio—Online-RLHF and Online-State-Constraint. In Figure 12(b) we plot those results for PBRR and the baselines that learn to repair a proxy reward function—RRM and RRM + State-Constraint. In Figure 13 we plot those results for the ablations from Figure 3.

K.7 PBRR with a pessimistic proxy reward function

In Section 4 we discuss a key assumption behind PBRR’s preference learning objective: the human-specified proxy reward function is either aligned or optimistic. Here we investigate PBRR’s performance in the AI safety gridworld when repairing a pessimistic proxy reward function. In particular, we construct a new proxy reward function that is the same as the proxy reward function used for the AI safety gridworld in Section 5, except that it assigns a negative reward for visiting 39\frac{3}{9} tomato-containing states—which the ground-truth reward function assigns a positive reward for visiting. As such, this proxy reward function breaks our optimism assumption. We plot the results in Figure 14. PBRR eventually attains near-optimal performance but requires more preferences than when repairing an optimistic proxy reward function, as assumed in Figure 2. We note that even when the optimism assumption does not hold, PBRR still outperforms other methods for repairing the proxy reward function.
